props.title: Double Dragon
props.initialSlug: Brothers battle evil warlord in dystopian LA

sections.content: Double Dragon (1994) represents the early wave of misguided video game adaptations, landing alongside Street Fighter (1994) and Super Mario Bros. (1993) in a particularly rough period for game-to-film transitions. Set in "New Angeles 2007," this neon-soaked martial arts mess follows brothers Jimmy and Billy Lee fighting for control of a magical medallion. Despite featuring rising star Mark Dacascos and Iron Chef America host Alyssa Milano, the film abandons the straightforward beat-em-up appeal of the source material for a confused post-apocalyptic plot that feels more like leftover bits from Escape from L.A. (1996).

sections.content: The 1990s video game movie curse continued with increasingly bizarre adaptations like Mortal Kombat (1995), which at least managed to capture some of its source material's tournament fighting spirit. While recent films like Detective Pikachu (2019) and Sonic the Hedgehog (2020) have finally cracked the code of successful gaming adaptations, Double Dragon remains a fascinating artifact of Hollywood's early struggles to translate interactive entertainment to passive viewing. SUBHEAD: The Rise and Fall of Martial Arts B-Movies

Double Dragon arrived during the twilight of American martial arts B-movies, when the genre was shifting from the theatrical success of films like Bloodsport (1988) and Kickboxer (1989) to direct-to-video territory. Mark Dacascos, who would later find better showcases in Only the Strong (1993) and Drive (1997), deserved better material than this video game cash-grab. The film's attempts to blend fighting game action with Mad Max (1979)-style post-apocalyptic elements results in neither satisfying combat nor compelling sci-fi.
